Has anyone played Bubble Bobble? My brother and I grew up playing it. One of the fun things about it was all the random things that would pop up. When you get started you don't know what to expect. There are items that give you bonus points like fruits and candies. Some items give you extra powers, and others do more unexpected things. But it turns out it's not totally random. You learn how to make certain items appear after a while (and of course, what they do). More clever players have even found ways to control some of the game's "random" events.

So how does a computer generate random events in the first place? In C there is a rand() function. Let's try it out:

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
int main()
{
 int i;
 for(i=0;i<20;i++)
 {
 printf("%d\n",rand());
 printf("\nPress enter.\n");
 getchar();
 
 }

 return 0;
}

You can paste and run the code here. It does what you might expect, it just prints random numbers. Where do these numbers come from? Well, if you pay attention to those numbers, you'll see it gives you the same twenty numbers every time you start it.

The first sequence of numbers most people learn goes: 1, 2, 3, 4... This sequence is generated simply by starting with 1 and adding 1 to the number you're on to produce the next number at each step. If we use different rules we can produce different sequences.

1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28, 36...

9, 8, 1, -12, -31, -56, -87...

We can produce sequences that look random from rules. The less obvious our rules are, the more random the sequence will look. Maybe this isn't true randomness though. If you go into a casino and throw dice, it won't land on the same thing for each move every time you play a new game. Let's see how Python does with dice:

#! /usr/bin/python

from random import randint #we'll need the random function for integers

class Die: #define the class of die 
 def __init__(self,numFaces): #can be initialized with a custom number of faces
 if numFaces<2:
 self.numFaces=2 #we'll use at least two faces
 else:
 self.numFaces = numFaces #you can choose a number >= 2
 self.faceValue=0

 def roll(self): #defines method to roll die
 self.faceValue=randint(1,self.numFaces) #select a random integer from 1 to the number of faces for the die
 return self.faceValue #and return the result of the roll

 def show(self): #show Unicode die face
 faces=[u'\u2680',u'\u2681',u'\u2682',u'\u2683',u'\u2684',u'\u2685'];
 if self.faceValue <= 6:
 print (str(self.faceValue)+": "+faces[self.faceValue-1])
 else:
 print (str(self.faceValue+1)+": "+self.faceValue)
 
 
# The main routine.
while 1:
 die=Die(6) #create our die
 die.roll()
 die.show()
 c=input("Continue? ")
 if c[0]!='y':
 exit()

You can paste and run this code here. If you run this code a few times, you'll see you get a different outcome every time you run it. So how is Python coming up with its random numbers? Let's see if we can do something like it in C.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <time.h>

int main()
{
 srand(time(0));
 int i;
 for(i=0;i<20;i++)
 {
 printf("%d\n",rand());
 printf("\nPress enter.\n");
 getchar();
 
 }

 return 0;
}
